question:
For Intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (OMIM #618089), caused by variants in FBXO11: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Clinical phenotypes reported in affected individuals with FBXO11-related intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (OMIM #618089), including exact cohort-specific counts (numerator and denominator per cohort, not percentages alone), original paper wording, standard HPO terms if identifiable, and citation with PMID or DOI.
Most discriminating clinical findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in overlapping/confusable disorders, including names of those disorders and the confidence of the distinction.
Findings looked for and found absent in affected individuals whose presence would argue against the diagnosis (pertinent negatives).
Analysis of whether phenotype differs by variant type, variant position, age, or sex.
Any findings or phenotypic characteristics that one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

FBXO11.definition: A gene encoding F-box protein 11, a member of the F-box protein family functioning as part of the SCF (SKP1-cullin-F-box) ubiquitin ligase complex. Heterozygous pathogenic variants in FBXO11, occurring predominantly de novo or in an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, cause intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (IDDFBA, OMIM #618089), a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by global developmental delay, intellectual disability, behavioral anomalies, hypotonia, facial dysmorphisms, and variable secondary features.

prior.text: A patient with FBXO11-related disorder cannot be uniquely diagnosed purely on a single pathognomonic sign; however, they can be differentiated from clinically overlapping syndromes by a combination of profound speech delay disproportionate to motor delay, severe externalizing behavioral disturbances (ADHD, impulsive/aggressive behaviors, sleep problems), and facial dysmorphisms (prominent forehead, broad/bulbous nasal tip, thin upper vermilion, and downslanting palpebral fissures), coupled with the distinct absence of progressive microcephaly, coarse facial features, severe visceral malformations, or hypoplastic distal phalanges/nails.
candidate_answers: In the index cohort reported by Gregor et al. 2018 (PMID: 30100085), speech and language impairment (HP:0000750) is near-universal (~100%, 14/14 individuals assessed), frequently presenting as absent speech or significant expressive language delay compared to motor milestones.

Behavioral abnormalities (HP:0000708) including hyperactivity/ADHD (HP:0007018), aggressive behavior (HP:0000718), and autistic traits or ASD (HP:0000729) are reported in approximately 70-80% of individuals in initial cohorts (e.g., Gregor et al. 2018), serving as key clinical features separating it from quiet or hypoactive syndromic ID presentations.

Recurrent craniofacial dysmorphisms include prominent forehead/frontal bossing (HP:0002007), broad nasal tip (HP:0000455), hypertelorism (HP:0000316) or telecanthus (HP:0000506), and thin upper lip vermilion (HP:0000219), present in >60-75% of reported cases in Gregor et al. 2018.

Discrimination against Coffin-Siris syndrome (ARID1B and related genes) relies on the absence of hypoplastic or absent fifth fingernails/toenails (HP:0001792/HP:0001800) and lack of generalized hypertrichosis (HP:0000998) in FBXO11 patients; discrimination against Koolen-de Vries syndrome (KANSL1) relies on the absence of a characteristic pear-shaped nose and hyper-affable personality.

Features that are consistently absent or rare (acting as negative discriminators) include progressive neurodegeneration, structural congenital limb-reduction deficiencies, complex congenital heart defects, and persistent profound microcephaly (head circumference is typically normal to mildly macrocephalic).

Most variants represent haploinsufficiency via de novo loss-of-function (frameshift, nonsense, canonical splice site mutations), while missense variants clustering in critical functional domains (such as the F-box or UBR domains) yield an indistinguishable core phenotype without proven distinct genotype-phenotype divergence to date.

d1.question_text: What are the precise numerators and denominators for each dysmorphic trait and behavioral symptom across all published FBXO11 cases since 2018?
d1.alloc_rationale: Directly tackles core question 1 by extracting exact cohort-specific numerators and denominators with HPO terms across all major published FBXO11 series.

d2.question_text: Do individuals harboring missense variants in specific functional domains of FBXO11 exhibit a milder or distinct phenotype compared to those with whole-gene deletions or truncating loss-of-function mutations?

d3.question_text: Are there any documented conflicting clinical findings regarding seizures or structural brain anomalies (e.g., corpus callosum hypoplasia) between early and recent cohorts?

d4.question_text: Does expressive language delay significantly exceed receptive language delay across all age groups and FBXO11 variant types?
d4.rationale: Goel et al. noted expressive language delay was more pronounced than receptive language impairment in several patients, but standardized receptive vs. expressive language assessment scores across different stages of development are needed to confirm a distinct dissociation.

d5.question_text: What distinguishes the facial gestalt and behavioral profile of FBXO11-related disorder from other F-box/ubiquitin ligase disorders such as FBXW7 and CUL1?
d5.rationale: Both CUL1 and FBXW7 cause overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotypes involving speech delay and facial dysmorphism; systematic computer-assisted facial analysis (GestaltMatcher) and deep phenotyping are needed to validate distinguishing clinical features.

d6.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Behavioral abnormalities (HP:0000708) including hyperactivity/ADHD (HP:0007018), aggressive behavior (HP:0000718), and autistic traits or ASD (HP:0000729) are reported in approximately 70-80% of individuals in initial cohorts (e.g., Gregor et al. 2018), serving as key clinical features separating it from quiet or hypoactive syndromic ID presentations.
d6.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Cohort penetrance discrepancy: Gregor et al. (2018) documented behavioral abnormalities in 85% (17/20) and preprint data reported 62% (13/21), whereas Pan et al. (2024) observed that in 12 Chinese individuals from 5 families, disruptive behavioral features were not present as a prevailing phenotype, with psychiatric disturbances limited to hallucinations in only 1/12 individuals.; Discriminative utility contradiction: The hypothesis claims behavioral hyperactivity/aggression reliably differentiates IDDFBA from hypoactive or quiet syndromic ID; however, hypotonia is present in up to 62% of cases, and familial cases demonstrate mild ID and dysmorphism without overt hyperactive or aggressive behavioral disruptions.
d6.alloc_rationale: Resolves key contradictions in behavioral phenotype penetrance between initial de novo cohorts and recent familial cohorts, addressing questions 2, 4, and 5.

d7.question_text: Does ascertainment bias in initial de novo pediatric cohorts inflate the perceived prevalence of externalizing behavioral abnormalities relative to adult or familial FBXO11 cases?
d7.rationale: Initial cohorts prioritized pediatric patients referred specifically for exome sequencing due to severe syndromic ID accompanied by refractory behavioral problems, whereas familial cohorts indicate significantly milder, non-disruptive cognitive presentations.

d8.question_text: Do specific missense variants in the CASH or UBR domains correlate with distinct neurobehavioral trajectories compared to protein-truncating loss-of-function variants in FBXO11?
d8.rationale: Functional cellular assays demonstrate domain-specific mislocalization patterns (nuclear exclusion vs. cytoplasmic aggregation), which may underlie intra-syndromic phenotypic variation between behavioral dysregulation and purely cognitive presentations.

d9.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Recurrent craniofacial dysmorphisms include prominent forehead/frontal bossing (HP:0002007), broad nasal tip (HP:0000455), hypertelorism (HP:0000316) or telecanthus (HP:0000506), and thin upper lip vermilion (HP:0000219), present in >60-75% of reported cases in Gregor et al. 2018.
d9.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While high/broad forehead, broad nasal tip, hypertelorism, and thin upper lip are recurrent dysmorphic descriptors in FBXO11 cohorts, cohort-wide facial dysmorphism is only present in 67% of patients overall (Goel et al.), contradicting the assertion that each of these individual features occurs at a 60-75% frequency.; Gregor et al. (2018) and Jansen et al. (2019) describe FBXO11-related facial dysmorphism as minor, subtle, and nonspecific, emphasizing that patients often lack an overt, easily recognizable facial gestalt from dysmorphism alone.

d10.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of computer vision facial gestalt tools (e.g., GestaltMatcher) in discriminating FBXO11-related disorder from other F-box and neurodevelopmental syndromes?
d10.rationale: Because individual dysmorphic features have moderate penetration (overall dysmorphism ~67%) and are individually nonspecific, objective automated facial phenotype modeling may delineate composite sub-visual gestalt markers.

d11.question_text: Do truncating/haploinsufficient FBXO11 variants produce a distinct craniofacial signature compared to domain-specific missense variants?
d11.rationale: Studies observe phenotypic pleiotropy (including TRPS-like phenocopies and severe ocular dysgenesis) with missense alleles; systematic correlation across all published cohorts will clarify phenotypic heterogeneity.

d12.question_text: What is the exact incidence and severity grade of cardiac and structural visceral defects across pooled international FBXO11 cohorts?
d12.rationale: Clarifying whether subclinical cardiac abnormalities exist on formal echocardiographic screening will strengthen the use of cardiac structural integrity as an exclusion criterion.

d13.question_text: Does longitudinal tracking of head circumference trajectories from birth into adulthood show progressive deceleration or stabilization in FBXO11-mutated patients?
d13.rationale: Documenting head circumference Z-scores over time would formalize head growth parameters for differential diagnosis against primary microcephaly syndromes.

d14.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Discrimination against Coffin-Siris syndrome (ARID1B and related genes) relies on the absence of hypoplastic or absent fifth fingernails/toenails (HP:0001792/HP:0001800) and lack of generalized hypertrichosis (HP:0000998) in FBXO11 patients; discrimination against Koolen-de Vries syndrome (KANSL1) relies on the absence of a characteristic pear-shaped nose and hyper-affable personality.
d14.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Published FBXO11 cohorts (Jansen et al. 2019, Gregor et al. 2022) emphasize that individuals present with subtle, non-specific dysmorphism without a distinct pathognomonic facial gestalt, making phenotypic-only discrimination from overlapping syndromes unreliable without genomic sequencing.; The available literature in the sources block provides no direct validation that Koolen-de Vries syndrome (KANSL1) can be reliably differentiated from FBXO11 purely based on the absence of pear-shaped nose or hyper-affability.

d15.question_text: Can computational deep-phenotyping algorithms (e.g., PhenoScore or GestaltMatcher) reliably discriminate FBXO11-associated facial features from Coffin-Siris syndrome and Koolen-de Vries syndrome cohorts?
d15.rationale: Because human clinical inspection often fails to identify distinct syndromic features in FBXO11, automated quantitative phenomic and facial analysis tools could determine whether subtle sub-visual facial dysmorphism patterns can distinguish them.

d16.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence of distal digital and nail hypoplasia in an aggregated international cohort of FBXO11 patients?
d16.rationale: Clarifying the exact penetrance of nail/phalanx anomalies across all documented FBXO11 patients will definitively test whether nail hypoplasia serves as an absolute negative discriminator against Coffin-Siris syndrome.

d19.question_text: Does the frequency of microcephaly (HP:0000252) versus macrocephaly (HP:0000256) differ by variant class (truncating loss-of-function vs missense) across pooled post-2018 FBXO11 cohorts?
d19.rationale: Goel et al. 2026 identified microcephaly in 24% of patients, whereas early publications reported normocephaly or mild relative macrocephaly, suggesting possible subphenotypic divergence.

d20.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence of ophthalmologic defects (e.g. strabismus, reduced visual acuity) and hearing impairment in FBXO11 patients when evaluated by protocolized screening?
d20.rationale: Pan et al. 2024 reported reduced visual acuity in 4/12 patients and recent case reports note strabismus and hearing impairment, indicating sensory involvement may be under-ascertained.

d21.question_text: Does the prevalence and severity of disruptive externalizing behaviors correlate with variant class (truncating/loss-of-function versus domain-specific missense variants) or inheritance mode (de novo vs familial transmission) in FBXO11?
d21.rationale: Ascertainment bias via de novo exome trios often selects for severe neurobehavioral manifestations, whereas familial inherited cases and certain missense variants may manifest with attenuated neurodevelopmental profiles.

d22.question_text: What is the systematic performance of combining craniofacial gestalt metrics with behavioral screening compared to behavioral screening alone in discriminating FBXO11 from overlapping ID syndromes?
d22.rationale: Recent computational phenotyping (e.g., GestaltMatcher in Goel et al. 2026) detected measurable facial similarity across FBXO11 individuals; evaluating its discrimination power when combined with neurobehavioral assessments would resolve whether behavioral variability impairs clinical diagnosis.

d23.question_text: Does subcellular partitioning difference between N-terminal/F-box variants (nuclear exclusion and degradation) and C-terminal UBR variants (cytoplasmic accumulation) translate into subtle differences in metabolic or growth phenotypes such as obesity?
d23.rationale: Gregor et al. (2022) identified distinct molecular cellular behaviors between domains and suggested possible correlations with obesity, warranting systematic metabolic evaluation across large cohorts.

d24.question_text: Can computational facial phenotyping (e.g., GestaltMatcher) reliably discriminate FBXO11-related disorder from clinically overlapping neurodevelopmental disorders sharing hypotonia and behavioral dysregulation?
d24.rationale: Because facial dysmorphism is subtle and cognitive phenotypes overlap broadly with other neurodevelopmental syndromes, objective quantitative gestalt scoring may facilitate pre-test syndromic identification.

d25.question_text: Is the TRPS-like presentation restricted exclusively to specific missense variants in the functional domains of FBXO11, or can loss-of-function (truncating/frameshift) variants also cause nail hypoplasia and cone-shaped epiphyses?
d25.rationale: Clarifying domain-specific genotype-phenotype correlations will determine whether TRPS phenocopies are unique to specific missense alleles (e.g., p.His594Arg acting via dominant-negative or neomorphic mechanisms) versus haploinsufficiency.

d26.question_text: Do FBXO11 truncating/nonsense variants versus missense variants localized to specific functional domains (e.g., F-box domain vs. UBR Zn-finger domain) correlate with the severity and penetrance of behavioral abnormalities?
d26.rationale: In vitro studies show differential subcellular localization and turnover depending on domain localization; systematically profiling behavioral phenotypes by variant domain will determine if behavioral dysregulation maps to specific sub-mechanisms.

d27.question_text: What proportion of adults harboring inherited FBXO11 variants meet formal diagnostic criteria for neuropsychiatric conditions compared to pediatric probands identified via de novo sequencing?
d27.rationale: Familial and older cohorts may exhibit milder or attenuated behavioral manifestations compared to pediatric probands ascertained specifically through autism/behavioral clinics, mitigating ascertainment bias.

d28.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Seizures occur in 25-45% of FBXO11 variant carriers, representing a substantially more frequent neurological feature than described in initial index cohorts and functioning as an active discriminating sign.
d28.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: The initial index cohort (Gregor et al. 2018) already observed seizures in 25% (5/20) of cases, directly contradicting the premise that subsequent cohorts identified a 'substantially more frequent' manifestation than initial descriptions.; Seizures cannot act as an active discriminating sign because they are absent in the majority (57-75%) of FBXO11 patients and represent a frequent, non-specific finding across competing intellectual developmental disorders (such as those described in Zacher et al. 2021 and Mainali et al. 2023).

d29.question_text: What specific electroclinical seizure semiology or EEG patterns, if any, distinguish FBXO11-related epilepsy from other monogenic neurodevelopmental syndromes?
d29.rationale: While seizure occurrence alone has low discriminating power (25-43%), specific epilepsy syndromes or characteristic EEG anomalies could provide true differential diagnostic utility.

d30.question_text: How do quantitative facial gestalt algorithms (e.g., GestaltMatcher) perform in differentiating FBXO11 from clinically overlapping intellectual disability syndromes?
d30.rationale: Goel et al. 2026 demonstrated measurable intra-cohort facial similarity, suggesting facial morphology may possess substantially higher discriminatory value than intermittent neurological signs like seizures.

d31.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: The simultaneous presence of axial/congenital hypotonia (HP:0001252) alongside disruptive behavioral disturbances (HP:0000708) is a distinctive signature of FBXO11-related disorder that differentiates it from non-syndromic ADHD or purely hyperactive neurobehavioral conditions.
d31.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Hypotonia prevalence varies sharply between cohorts, ranging from 60-62% in Goel et al. (2026) and Jansen et al. (2019) down to only 1 of 12 (8.3%) in Pan et al. (2024).; Neither hypotonia nor behavioral disturbances are fully penetrant (both ~62% in Goel et al.), meaning substantial subsets of FBXO11 patients lack one or both features.

d32.question_text: Does the prevalence of hypotonia in FBXO11-related disorder depend on variant position (e.g., CASH domain vs. UBR domain vs. truncating variants)?
d32.rationale: Gregor et al. (2022) revealed domain-specific functional consequences on protein localization and degradation, which may correlate with the presence or absence of neuromuscular features like hypotonia.

d33.question_text: Is the low reported frequency of hypotonia in certain cohorts (e.g., Pan et al., 2024) an artifact of ascertainment at older ages or a true population/variant-specific divergence?
d33.rationale: Congenital hypotonia often improves with age into childhood/adulthood; retrospective phenotyping in older cohorts may under-ascertain early-life hypotonia.

d34.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: The neurobehavioral phenotype in FBXO11 deficiency exhibits longitudinal age-dependent evolution, transitioning from childhood hyperactive/aggressive dysregulation (ADHD, temper tantrums) to adolescent and adult internalizing psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety and depression.
d34.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Externalizing symptoms (hyperactivity, ADHD, and aggressive behavioral issues) persist into late adolescence (e.g. at 14 years of age in Fritzen et al. 2018) and adulthood (Mainali et al. 2023), contradicting a mandatory evolutionary transition where externalizing traits remit in favor of internalizing symptoms.; Internalizing symptoms (anxiety) and externalizing symptoms (ADHD, aggression) are reported as co-occurring behavioral characteristics in cross-sectional pediatric/adolescent series (Jansen et al. 2019) rather than chronologically separated stages.

d35.question_text: Does standardized longitudinal psychiatric assessment in a multi-center cohort of FBXO11 mutation carriers reveal true age-dependent symptom evolution versus lifetime cumulative comorbidity?
d35.rationale: Available evidence relies on retrospective chart reviews and cross-sectional snapshots; formal prospective tracking using validated instruments across childhood, adolescence, and adulthood is required to assess whether hyperactivity shifts to depression.

d36.question_text: Do truncating loss-of-function versus missense variants in FBXO11 differentially correlate with persistent externalizing ADHD phenotypes versus predominant affective disorders?
d36.rationale: Phenotypic heterogeneity across reported cohorts may stem from allelic heterogeneity (missense vs nonsense/frameshift) rather than strictly chronological patient age.

d37.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Overt craniofacial dysmorphism is penetrant in only approximately two-thirds of FBXO11-related disorder cases (ca. 60-67%) and can be subtle or clinically non-evident, rather than serving as an obligatory diagnostic hallmark across all affected cohorts.
d37.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Published literature review calculates the penetrance of facial dysmorphism at 78%, which exceeds the hypothesized 60-67% ceiling, whereas the newest series of 21 patients observes exactly 67% (14/21), indicating ascertainment variability between initial descriptions and expanded series.

d38.question_text: Does computer-aided objective facial gestalt analysis (e.g., GestaltMatcher) detect subtle sub-clinical facial signatures in FBXO11 variant carriers who are clinically designated as non-dysmorphic?
d38.rationale: Clinical dysmorphology evaluations are subjective and prone to ascertainment bias; automated deep phenotyping across all published and newly assembled cohorts would standardize dysmorphism rates.

d39.question_text: Is the presence or absence of facial dysmorphism correlated with variant class (e.g., missense vs. truncating/loss-of-function) or variant domain position in FBXO11?
d39.rationale: Determining whether missense variants that alter protein localization/expression correlate with different dysmorphology rates compared to haploinsufficiency-causing nonsense/frameshift variants will refine diagnostic accuracy.

d40.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Increased body weight or obesity (HP:0001513) is a recurrent feature in FBXO11-related disorder that occurs in over 50% of specific cohorts, distinguishing it from syndromic intellectual disability entities characterized by growth failure or cachexia.
d40.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Increased body weight exceeded 50% in one familial Chinese cohort (7/12, 58.3%), but occurred in only 25% (5/20) and 17.4% (4/23) in larger multicenter cohorts of de novo FBXO11 variants.; Short stature and impaired somatic growth occur in 50% (6/12) of the Chinese cohort and 20% (4/20) of the initial Gregor cohort, contradicting the notion that the syndrome is uniformly distinguishable from growth-failure entities.

d41.question_text: Does FBXO11 variant type (loss-of-function/truncating vs missense) systematically govern metabolic phenotype vs growth failure?
d41.rationale: Gregor et al. (2022) observed that overweight/hyperphagia was enriched in likely gene disrupting (LGD) variants compared to missense variants, which could explain differing frequencies across cohorts.

d42.question_text: Is increased body weight in FBXO11-related disorder age-dependent, emerging primarily in older children and adolescents rather than infants?
d42.rationale: Neurodevelopmental obesity syndromes often present with early hypotonia and feeding difficulties in infancy followed by hyperphagia and weight gain in later childhood.

d43.question_text: What specific receptive versus expressive language discrepancies and non-verbal communication abilities exist in FBXO11-related disorder compared to other E3-ubiquitin ligase neurodevelopmental syndromes?
d43.rationale: Speech delay is 95-100% penetrant in FBXO11, but distinguishing whether comprehension is preserved relative to verbal expression will refine clinical differential diagnosis against syndromes like Angelman (UBE3A).

d44.question_text: What specific facial biometric traits identified by computational facial analysis (e.g., GestaltMatcher, PhenoScore) provide objective discrimination of FBXO11 from clinically overlapping chromatin/ubiquitin disorders?
d44.rationale: Facial dysmorphism is noted in only ~67% of individuals and is clinically subtle; objective machine-learning facial phenotyping may detect sub-visual discriminative features separating it from ARID1B or KANSL1.

d45.question_text: Does variant class (likely gene-disrupting/nonsense/frameshift versus missense) correlate specifically with microcephaly versus macrocephaly in FBXO11-related disorder?
d45.rationale: Gregor et al. (2018) suggested that microcephaly was enriched in individuals with likely gene-disrupting variants compared to missense variants, whereas Lee et al. (2020) observed macrocephaly in a frameshift duplication family. Clarifying this will determine whether cranial size variations reflect distinct molecular mechanisms.

d46.question_text: What is the true prevalence and spectrum of cleft palate, bifid uvula, and velopharyngeal insufficiency in FBXO11-related disorder across all published cohorts?
d46.rationale: Cleft palate/bifid uvula is reported in 3/20 patients in Gregor et al. (2018) and could serve as an affirmative discriminator from other behavioral/ID conditions if penetrant at >10-15%.

d47.question_text: Do truncating/loss-of-function FBXO11 mutations correlate with microcephaly whereas specific missense mutations or gain-of-function variants associate with normal or macrocephalic head circumference?
d47.rationale: Determining genotype-phenotype correlations between mutation class/domain location and cranial biometry will clarify why a quarter develop microcephaly while others have normal or increased head circumference.

d48.question_text: Is microcephaly in FBXO11 deficiency predominantly postnatal/secondary due to brain growth deceleration or congenital/primary?
d48.rationale: Serial head circumference measurements from birth through adolescence across pooled international registries will determine the exact developmental trajectory of microcephaly in affected individuals.

d49.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Speech delay and expressive language impairment (HP:0000750) is the single most sensitive phenotypic marker for FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder, exhibiting penetrance of at least 95% across expanded independent cohorts and consistently outperforming behavioral dysregulation and facial dysmorphism in clinical sensitivity.
d49.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Pan et al. (2024) observed speech and language developmental delay in only 8 of 12 (66.7%) affected individuals from 5 families, contradicting the hypothesis that speech delay maintains a penetrance of >=95% across independent expanded cohorts.; In Pan et al. (2024), intellectual disability was present in 100% (12/12) and global developmental delay in 83.3% (10/12), demonstrating that general cognitive delay/ID can have higher clinical sensitivity than speech impairment in certain familial cohorts.

d50.question_text: Does speech impairment penetrance in FBXO11 disorder differ between familial/inherited hypomorphic variants versus de novo loss-of-function variants?
d50.rationale: Familial cases like those in Pan et al. (2024) showed reduced penetrance of speech delay (66.7%), whereas de novo truncating and severe missense cohorts showed 95-100% speech delay. Stratifying penetrance by inheritance and variant class will clarify diagnostic utility.

patterns.pattern: Diagnostic discrimination in syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders often relies on the structural non-involvement of organ systems rather than positive cognitive hallmarks
patterns.abstraction: When neurodevelopmental impairments are ubiquitous across distinct genetic syndromes, exclusionary value derives from organ-specific anatomical spares rather than cognitive manifestations
patterns.instance: FBXO11-related disorder exhibits near-zero penetrance for complex congenital heart defects (HP:0001627) and congenital limb-reduction deficiencies (0/21 in Goel et al.; 0/12 in Pan et al.), differentiating it from phenotypically overlapping conditions like Cornelia de Lange or Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes
